approachQuestion.prompt:
Long serial check

A serial is a nonempty read-only decimal digit string, possibly with leading zeros. Return the remainder of its represented nonnegative integer divided by positive m.

Example 1: serial="001234",m=17 -> 10.
Example 2: serial="000",m=7 -> 0.

Constraints and assumptions: 1 <= n <= 200000 digits; 1 <= m <= 10^9. The represented integer need not fit a machine word. Digit access costs one operation. Do not modify the string. Choose the best time bound among the offered correct methods, then the least auxiliary storage when time ties.

options.text: Scan digits left to right with r=0; update r=(10*r+digit) mod m.
options.feedback: Appending digit d multiplies the previous prefix by ten and adds d; modular equivalence preserves the bounded residue.

options.text: Use the same recurrence, store every prefix residue in a fresh array, and return the last.
options.feedback: Every residue is correct, but only the preceding one is needed; the array is removable.

options.text: Return the sum of digits modulo m.
options.feedback: For "12" and m=7 it returns 3 instead of 5; place values matter.

options.text: Parse only the final nine digits and reduce modulo m.
options.feedback: For "1000000000" and m=7 it returns 0 instead of 6; higher positions contribute.

feedback.reason: Maintain the residue of an arbitrarily long decimal prefix.
details: Start r=0. Read left to right, replacing r with (10*r+digit) mod m. Return r.
Appending digit d changes a number's residue to (10*r+d) mod m. The full integer need not fit or be stored. Processing digits in reverse would assign different place values.
“Scan digits left to right with r=0; update r=(10*r+digit) mod m.”: Appending digit d multiplies the previous prefix by ten and adds d; modular equivalence preserves the bounded residue.
“Use the same recurrence, store every prefix residue in a fresh array, and return the last.”: Every residue is correct, but only the preceding one is needed; the array is removable.
“Return the sum of digits modulo m.”: For "12" and m=7 it returns 3 instead of 5; place values matter.
“Parse only the final nine digits and reduce modulo m.”: For "1000000000" and m=7 it returns 0 instead of 6; higher positions contribute.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze only the revealed method (prefix-residue). Let n be the number of digits. Choose its tightest standard worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair.
constraints: Exact signed 64-bit words. Since r<m<=10^9, 10*r+digit<10^10 fits. Remainder and digit access cost one operation.
Iterative method, no recursion or hashing, no input copies. Auxiliary space includes all temporary state and buffers, excluding supplied input and returned output.
Include initialization and any copying; no hidden preprocessing or cache.

options.text: O(log n) time, O(1) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: Each decimal digit updates one bounded residue.
details: The scan processes all n digits once and stores only the current residue and index. For legal m such as 7 every digit can affect the answer, so the scan has linear worst-case time.
Exact signed 64-bit words. Since r<m<=10^9, 10*r+digit<10^10 fits. Remainder and digit access cost one operation.
Iterative method, no recursion or hashing, no input copies. Auxiliary space includes all temporary state and buffers, excluding supplied input and returned output.
“O(n) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: Correct: one bounded update per digit.
“O(n) time, O(n) auxiliary space”: This describes saving all prefix residues, which this method avoids.
“O(log n) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: The recurrence visits every digit.
“O(n²) time, O(n) auxiliary space”: No prefix is reparsed and no string is copied.
